analysis.one_liner: Shields earned income tax credit payments from lenders and collectors, and bans refund-anticipation loan debt collection and forced arbitration.
analysis.headline: The Senate never voted on the bill; it was sent to the Finance Committee in April 2007 and died there at the end of the 110th Congress with just two cosponsors.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would protect working families who receive the earned income tax credit, a refund for low- and moderate-wage workers. It would stop creditors from seizing or assigning those payments, stop lenders from using refund-anticipation loans to collect a customer's old debts, and ban forced arbitration clauses in those loans. It would also shut down an IRS program that told tax preparers whether a customer's refund would be seized, which helped lenders sell costly refund-anticipation products, and it would direct Treasury to promote a cheaper path: getting the credit spread through the year and setting up low-cost bank or credit union accounts.
analysis.who_benefits: Low- and moderate-income workers who claim the earned income tax credit. Their refunds would be protected from garnishment and from lenders who arrange refund-anticipation loans so that old debts come off the top of the refund before the family sees a dime. They would also keep the right to go to court instead of forced arbitration if a refund-anticipation lender cheats them.

how_it_helps.text: EITC payments would become non-transferable and immune to garnishment, attachment, or offset by anyone except the federal government, and any waiver of that protection would be null and void. [S2] [S3]

Debt collectors would be barred from collecting a delinquent debt out of a federal tax refund by arranging a refund-anticipation loan or refund-anticipation check with a built-in repayment offset. [S2] [S3]
Lenders linked to federal tax refunds could no longer make mandatory arbitration a condition of the loan. [S2] [S3]
The IRS Debt Indicator program would be terminated; that program signaled to preparers whether a taxpayer's refund would be reduced, which enabled high-fee refund-anticipation products. [S2] [S3]

Treasury would run programs encouraging greater use of the advance EITC and would set up cooperative agreements with federally insured banks and credit unions to offer low- and moderate-income taxpayers low-cost direct deposit accounts. [S2] [S3]

analysis.who_pays: Refund-anticipation loan lenders and the tax-preparation chains that sell those loans and checks would lose a high-fee product, and debt collectors would lose one route to seizing refunds. Banks and credit unions would be asked to offer low-cost accounts instead, with federal cooperation.

drawbacks.text: Some families rely on refund-anticipation loans to get cash quickly before the refund arrives; restricting the product removes a (very expensive) source of fast money and assumes Treasury's low-cost account programs fill the gap. [S2] [S3]
The bill authorizes open-ended appropriations for two new Treasury programs with no spending cap. [S3]
It excludes returns filed with refund-anticipation loans from the IRS's electronic-filing goal count, weakening a metric the IRS uses to push e-filing adoption. [S2] [S3]

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The consumer protections target products whose fees were famously high relative to the small, short-term loans involved, and the cheaper alternatives the bill promotes (advance EITC payments and low-cost insured accounts) would serve the same need at a fraction of the cost. The honest cost is transition friction: families who used these loans for immediate cash would need a substitute, and the bill's success would depend on Treasury programs that were untested. On balance the protections outweigh the cost for the people involved.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate read the bill twice, sent it to the Finance Committee, and no one ever brought it up again before the 110th Congress ended in January 2009.

narrative.text: Sen. Akaka introduced the bill on April 17, 2007, with Sen. Bingaman and Sen. Durbin. [S3] [S5]
The bill was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Finance; the record shows no hearing, markup, vote, or further action of any kind. [S5] [S1]
The bill attracted only two cosponsors and never left committee, and it expired when the 110th Congress ended. [S4] [S5] [S1]

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Refund-anticipation lenders, tax-preparation chains selling those loans and checks, and debt collectors who used refund offsets kept their fee income. Families claiming the EITC kept paying the fees the bill would have ended.

for.name: Sen. Daniel Akaka
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and was its lead sponsor.

for.name: Sens. Jeff Bingaman and Dick Durbin
for.what_they_did: Joined as original cosponsors; the bill finished with only two cosponsors.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken. The sponsor and both cosponsors were Democrats, and the record contains no recorded opposition, only inaction.

industries.note: These lenders earned high fees advancing refunds to EITC families, and the bill would ban using those loans to collect a customer's old debts, ban mandatory arbitration clauses, and cut off the IRS Debt Indicator that supported the product. Their gain came directly at the cost of the refund families the bill protects.
Preparers earned fees on refund-anticipation loans and checks alongside the lenders; ending those products would remove a major add-on revenue stream at tax time.
The bill would close off one method of collecting delinquent consumer debts out of federal tax refunds, making EITC refunds unavailable to private creditors.

Treasury would sign cooperative agreements with federally insured depository institutions to offer low-cost direct deposit accounts, steering low-income taxpayers toward them as the cheaper alternative to refund loans.
